segments.text: It's a beautiful day, so you decide to go for a hike. Suddenly a snowstorm begins and you become disoriented and lost. The cold is overwhelming. Your fingers are numb, and you're feeling tired. Oh, so tired. You realize this is dangerous. What are you going to do? Hypothermia happens when your body rapidly loses heat and drops to a temperature of 35 °C (95 °F) or less. You'll begin shivering, become confused and feel sleepy. Eventually, your skin will turn blue. Your breathing and pulse will slow

and you could fall into a coma and die. On average, 4.6 million people worldwide die every year due to extreme cold. That accounts for 9% of all deaths. You should always dress appropriately for the weather outside. If it's cold, be sure to wear warm,

loose clothing. Layering clothes will also help you stay warm. Cover all areas of your skin. That includes wearing a hat, gloves and an appropriately warm jacket. Don't choose your clothing based on the amount of time you plan to be outside, especially if you expect it to be short. Dress for being outside a great deal longer than you plan on. In other words, dress for the unexpected.

As your temperature drops, your teeth will chatter. This is your body trying to keep you warm. You pick up your pace to stay warm. But your legs are beginning to fail and you stumble around. And you become disoriented. You feel so tired. So very tired. You can get your energy back with a short nap in a snowbank, right? No. Do not lie down or close your eyes. You won't get back up. If you start feeling cold and shivering, get into a warm, dry place. Change into dry, warm clothes if you can, especially if the clothes you're wearing are damp. A beverage that's sweet,

warm and without caffeine will help warm you from the inside. Broth is a good choice too. Do not drink alcohol or coffee. Alcohol only makes you lose heat faster, and coffee will put an extra strain on your heart. Extra layers, like a warm blanket, will help keep you toasty. If you're still not feeling well and have a rapid heart rate or shallow breathing, you'll need medical help, immediately. You don't need to be in a snowstorm to get hypothermia. Cold water can quickly remove heat from your body. Hypothermia is the leading cause of death by drowning. If you're in a large body of water and you can feel the cold setting in, don't panic. First, you'll need to keep your head above the water. Take deep breaths to stay buoyant. Wearing a life jacket helps keeps you afloat and it will help keep you warm.

Getting into the H.E.L.P. position or Heat Exchange Lessening Position will radiate your warmth back into your body. Bring your knees up to your chest, and keep your arms crossed around them. Only remove your clothing if it weighs you down. It will help insulate you from the cold. Call for help. But conserve your energy, and don't try swimming to shore unless you are absolutely certain you can reach it. If you come across someone suffering from hypothermia, call medical help right away. Get them to a dry shelter where they can get warm. Remove any wet clothing and wrap the person in dry towels, coats or blankets. Putting warm, not hot, water in a plastic bottle can help too. Instead of rubbing or massaging the person, which will increase tissue damage, use gentle skin-to-skin contact to transfer some of your heat to their body. Don't try to heat the hypothermia victim too quickly. Using electric lamps or hot water only damage tissue, especially if they are suffering from frostbite. Now that you know how to survive hypothermia, do you know how to survive severe heat? We'll show you what you need to do if you get sunburn on another episode of How To Survive.
